A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same gRNAde multi-state RNA design framework. Their main texts, appendices, equations, figures and tables are readable and support reliable comparison despite the changed title and expanded scope.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations across three data splits and a theophylline aptamer case study, including numerical sequence-recovery results in Tables 1–2.

after.justification: v4 reports original gRNAde evaluations, ablations, nucleotide-level analyses and retrospective fitness-ranking simulations. Rosetta and FARNA results are explicitly attributed to prior work.

M1.justification: The multi-state GVP encoder, conformer averaging and autoregressive decoder remain. Graph construction changes from C4' coordinates with 10 neighbors to three-bead centroids with 32 neighbors, and edge encodings increase from 16 to 32 channels. v4 also describes distance/angle/torsion features and evaluates a one-shot MLP decoder variant. These refine the retained architecture.

E1.justification: v4 expands beyond inverse-folding recovery to zero-shot fitness ranking on 74,943 RNA polymerase ribozyme variants, adding experimental fitness data and a distinct prediction task (Section 4.3). The dedicated ensemble-size evaluation and theophylline case study from v1 are no longer reported. RNASolo remains the inverse-design data source.

E2.justification: v1 principally compares multi-state gRNAde with its single-state variant. v4 adds Rosetta and FARNA comparisons using published recovery values, plus fitness-ranking baselines that randomly select from all variants, single mutants, or single and double mutants. Appendix Table 2 additionally compares autoregressive and one-shot decoders.

E3.justification: v4 replaces the three original splits with structurally clustered single-/multi-state splits using TM-score >0.45, and changes validation/test sizes from 200 to 100 each. Resolution filtering changes from 3 to 4 Å, and sampled designs from 100 to 16 per example. It adds MCC/perplexity metrics and screening-budget evaluation, while changing encoder/decoder depth from 3 to 4 layers, training from 100 to at most 50 epochs, and initial learning rate from 0.001 to 0.0001.

E4.justification: State-count comparisons continue, but v4 adds decoder-type and maximum-training-length ablations (Appendix Table 2), recovery analyses by nucleotide pairing, solvent accessibility and RMSD (Figure 6), and a perplexity–recovery analysis (Figure 4). The detailed theophylline case study in v1 Table 2 is removed.

E5.justification: Three-seed model evaluation is retained, with v4 explicitly identifying standard deviations. The new fitness study extends uncertainty reporting through 10,000 simulations per randomized strategy and screening budget. Figure 7 specifies medians and interquartile ranges, although the surrounding text calls the intervals confidence intervals. This does not establish an increase in training runs.

E6.justification: The original splitwise and theophylline results are replaced by new benchmark, ablation and fitness-ranking findings. v4 Appendix Table 1 reports recovery of 0.5682 for gRNAde versus 0.45 for Rosetta and 0.32 for FARNA. In its multi-state split, one-to-five-state mean recovery rises from 0.4549 to 0.4722, while mean MCC falls from 0.5689 to 0.5488 (Appendix Table 2). Changed protocols prevent interpreting these as performance changes relative to v1.

T1.justification: v4 adds an explicit distinction between the SO(3)-equivariant encoder with dihedral inputs and its O(3)-equivariant GVP layers. Section 4.2 also introduces a numerical probability-averaging counterexample; it does not establish the accompanying criticism of logit averaging because it averages probabilities. The main pooling mathematics remains, without substantial new theorem or proof development.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion expand from multi-state recovery gains to claims of superior single-state recovery and speed over Rosetta, support for partial design, and zero-shot mutant prioritization. Partial/masked design, previously presented as future work, becomes an advertised capability. The original multi-state representation-learning contribution remains.

C2.justification: v4 adds interpretations of benefits in flexible/exposed nucleotides and of autoregressive decoding improving self-consistency. It discusses limitations of recovery and secondary-structure proxies, increased multi-state memory costs, and fitness-ranking advantages restricted to low screening budgets. New applicability limits include interacting RNA chains, ligand interactions, negative design and control of conformational propensities. Wet-lab validation remains future work.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's basic hyperparameters and encoder pseudocode, v4 documents cross-entropy training, teacher forcing, label smoothing, coordinate noise, dropout, sampling temperature and parameter count. It supplies the RNASolo snapshot date, A100 hardware, training time and state-dependent memory costs. These substantially expand reproducibility information; newly disclosed settings alone do not establish procedural changes.

R1.justification: v4 adds a substantial related-work appendix covering energy-based inverse folding, backbone generation, structure prediction and RNA language models, including RNA FM, RiNaLMo and CodonBERT. It develops comparisons with Rosetta and positions gRNAde as a structure-conditioned language model, substantially extending v1's shorter RNA-versus-protein motivation.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten. The method becomes a structured exposition of the problem, representation, architecture and metrics; results are organized into three application sections. Separate related-work and usage-FAQ appendices substantially reorganize and expand the narrative around retained technical material.

P2.justification: v4 changes the main layout from two columns to one, redraws the pipeline and adds feature, architecture, evaluation and tensor-symmetry diagrams. New benchmark, nucleotide-analysis and fitness plots accompany redesigned result tables. The dataset-statistics display is retained and updated as Figure 9; the theophylline structure/sequence-logo table is removed.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evidence previously centered on recovery against its own single-state baseline. Structural-cluster holdouts, comparisons with published Rosetta/FARNA results, controlled ablations and retrospective fitness analysis improve assessment of generalization and practical utility. Expanded technical details and explicit limitations also improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: Rosetta runtime superiority is not established by controlled timing, and Figure 5's single-seed self-consistency benefit does not persist in the three-seed means in Appendix Table 2.
